item.title: Meta’s Muse AI agents could pose longer-term risk to loss costs: Autonomous
item.dc:creator: Beth Musselwhite
item.category: Artificial intelligence in insurance and reinsurance news
item.description:
Meta’s Muse AI agents may pose a longer-term risk to loss costs if savvy consumers use them to navigate, and potentially litigate, insurance claims, according to Autonomous analysts. In a recent report, Autonomous put Meta’s Muse to work across shopping, payments, deposit management, investing and insurance to assess what AI assistants can do with consumers’ […]

The post Meta’s Muse AI agents could pose longer-term risk to loss costs: Autonomous appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Meta’s Muse AI agents may pose a longer-term risk to loss costs if savvy consumers use them to navigate, and potentially litigate, insurance claims, according to Autonomous analysts.

In a recent report, Autonomous put Meta’s Muse to work across shopping, payments, deposit management, investing and insurance to assess what AI assistants can do with consumers’ money today.

For insurance specifically, Autonomous tested Muse’s ability to shop for auto, renters’ and even micro commercial insurance.

Analysts found that Muse sent timely reminders of the mandatory actions needed to get claims moving and even connected them with several law firms that might be able to help maximise a personal auto claim.

The report also found that agentic AI may increase price transparency for simple consumer insurance products.

Autonomous noted that its agent had mixed results fetching real insurance quotes. However, once it was fed the right data, Muse did a decent job summarising various insurance quotes, comparing and contrasting coverage, price, and discount potential.

As consumers increasingly focus on affordability, AI may give insurance buyers greater price transparency and help them make more informed purchasing decisions.

However, Autonomous noted that although Muse could help consumers become smarter insurance buyers, it does not yet outperform an insurance agent.

“Interfacing with our agent was more leisurely than pulling our own quotes from a bunch of different sites, and agentic AI equipped us with information which previously might have been considered ‘inside baseball’ for the average insurance consumer. However, agentic AI doesn’t do anything we couldn’t have accomplished by leveraging an agent or a comparative rater platform,” said Autonomous analysts.

Autonomous believes that underwriters likely to benefit most from the rise of agentic AI are those with a developed direct-to-consumer strategy that are quickest to develop a policy rate plug-in for the most popular platforms, while hindering those that still rely on agents, particularly captives.

Autonomous also warned that agentic AI raises concerns over consumer data privacy and inflated acquisition costs, with many platforms opting to limit Muse’s access.

Analysts added, “AI clearly can help educate and empower people to get more out of their insurance, and we continue to expect potential disruption to extend beyond the shopping process. To the extent agentic AI better informs and enables consumers to execute on rote tasks, we expect consumer willingness to submit and fight for a claim to increase, potentially driving an uptick in frequency and attorney representation. Indeed, perhaps the most severe risk, in our view, posed by agentic and generative AI to the insurance industry is that of increased lawyer involvement. While one may typically think of ambulance chasers, aggressive plaintiffs bars, and sympathetic juries as common drivers of tort inflation, we hypothesise AI in its many forms may need to be added to the list.”

The post Meta’s Muse AI agents could pose longer-term risk to loss costs: Autonomous appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

Homm takes up her new position on March 1st, 2027, and brings almost 20 years of industry experience to her new role. She has a […]

The post Munich Re’s American Modern names Homm President and CEO appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
American Modern Insurance Group, a specialty insurer and part of global reinsurer Munich Re, has appointed Angela Homm as its new President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO), succeeding Kevin Morreale.

Homm takes up her new position on March 1st, 2027, and brings almost 20 years of industry experience to her new role. She has a decade of leadership experience at American Modern across internal audit, accounting, regulatory compliance, and enterprise risk management.

Since 2018, Homm has held a range of senior leadership positions across Munich Re’s global organisation. This includes Global Chief Financial Officer and North American Chief Operating Officer for Munich Re Digital Partners, Chief Risk Officer for U.S. Property & Casualty Operations, and currently, Head of Finance Transformation for Global Specialty Insurance.

Morreale will continue to serve as Interim President and CEO through February 2027 before returning to his role as Chief Sales and Marketing Officer.

Mike Kerner, Member of the Board of Management, Munich Re, responsible for Global Specialty Insurance, said: “Angela is an exceptional leader whose deep understanding of American Modern, combined with her broad experience across Munich Re’s regional and global operations, makes her ideally positioned to lead the company into its next phase of growth.

“She brings a strong strategic mindset, operational expertise and a proven ability to drive transformation. We are confident that she will lead the American Modern team to build on our strong market position while delivering value for customers, partners and employees.”

The post Munich Re’s American Modern names Homm President and CEO appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.title: For legacy, discipline should sustain, not constrain growth: RiverStone International CEO
item.dc:creator: Luke Gallin
item.description:
During a fireside chat at the annual AIRROC conference in New Jersey yesterday, Paul Brockman, CEO of legacy specialist RiverStone International, highlighted the difference in underwriting discipline between the live and retrospective markets, emphasising that discipline should sustain rather than constrain growth. The second day of the 2026 AIRROC conference, which brings together re/insurance professionals […]

The post For legacy, discipline should sustain, not constrain growth: RiverStone International CEO appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
During a fireside chat at the annual AIRROC conference in New Jersey yesterday, Paul Brockman, CEO of legacy specialist RiverStone International, highlighted the difference in underwriting discipline between the live and retrospective markets, emphasising that discipline should sustain rather than constrain growth.

The second day of the 2026 AIRROC conference, which brings together re/insurance professionals to discuss the legacy market, was a day of insightful and thought-provoking panels and educational discussions. The opening fireside chat saw Rebecca Wilkinson, Restructuring Director at PwC, discuss market conditions with Brockman, who has more than 33 years of experience in insurance and reinsurance.

Brockman, who joined RiverStone International as Group CEO from Enstar in January 2026, explained that, alongside getting to know the company, its culture and its people, a main effort since taking on the role has been shifting the focus from a reactive to a proactive approach, a vision shared by his colleagues.

“What wasn’t a surprise was the quality of people that founded the company. RiverStone International has been around for a long time now, and has been particularly successful over the last four, five years. The scale of the opportunity in front of us was something that has probably surprised me a bit, in terms of we’ve seen unprecedented deal flow this year, and we wanted to be in a position that we could take advantage of that,” said Brockman.

Alongside the internal aspects, Wilkinson highlighted the external market environment as another important element for Brockman to focus on as he leads a large and growing, global legacy company. She noted the softening reinsurance market landscape, which has accelerated this year, and asked Brockman how he’s seeing the softening conversation play out in the legacy sector.

“I think it changes the conversation quite a lot, because in a hard market, it’s all about recycling the capital and insurers and reinsurers being able to use their capital to redeploy into a hard market. As a market we respond quite well to that environment. But now, when you go into a softer market, the conversation changes a bit. Insurers and reinsurers are thinking a bit more about ‘okay, which portfolios are performing well, which ones aren’t?’ And how do they use their capital a bit more efficiently,” said Brockman.

He went on to explain that uncertainty always accelerates the conversation as well.

“Legacy now, for us, it’s almost like the perfect environment because not only do you have capital drivers, you do deals to take away earnings volatility. We’re also in that softer phase of the cycle where organic growth is more difficult for insurers and reinsurers, so that should stimulate a bit more M&A activity. M&A activity is always good for this market, either before deals get done or afterwards, because I think what investors want going forward is that certainty. We always seize the fallout around that as well.

“So, the conversation has changed, but I think that’s good for us because all the drivers are in play, and a carefully constructed legacy transaction can deal with capital relief, it can deal with earnings volatility.”

In the softening phase of the market cycle, underwriting discipline is always a hot topic as competition intensifies in the live market and the focus on rate and terms and conditions increases.

While discipline is important in all parts of the re/insurance market through the cycle, Brockman emphasised that, for the legacy space, discipline is slightly different to the live market.

“For us, it’s about challenging claims assumptions, it’s about challenging reserving, market perception, litigation, legal interpretations,” said Brockman. “The way to look at discipline is it’s not something that should constrain your growth; it’s something that should sustain your growth.”

In terms of future deal activity, Brockman again noted unprecedented deal flow this year for RiverStone International, highlighting the company’s reactive approach across all of its platforms.

“Jurisdictionally, in the UK, Lloyd’s, Europe, Bermuda, the US, Australia, we’ve utilised all of our platforms. We’ve seen quite a lot of diversity in terms of the deals we’ve done across lines of business, and we’ve seen quite a lot of diversity in terms of structures and different parts of the market,” he said.

The post For legacy, discipline should sustain, not constrain growth: RiverStone International CEO appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

Isted joins Rokstone after four years at Antares Managing Agency Ltd, where she advanced from Assistant Underwriter to Underwriter in April 2024. She entered the insurance industry in 2018 through […]

The post Rokstone expands Specialty Reinsurance team amid growth plans appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Rokstone, an international managing general agent (MGA) specialising in specialty re/insurance, has appointed Airlie Isted ACII as an underwriter in its growing Specialty Reinsurance division.

Isted joins Rokstone after four years at Antares Managing Agency Ltd, where she advanced from Assistant Underwriter to Underwriter in April 2024.

She entered the insurance industry in 2018 through an apprenticeship at AXA XL, working in Specialty Reinsurance before progressing to a Trainee Underwriter role. Rokstone said her background includes experience in Marine, Energy and Terrorism reinsurance.

Isted has built her underwriting career through a series of progressive roles, becoming an underwriter at 23. Her move to Rokstone also brings her back into a working relationship with Eddie Hughes, the company’s Head of Specialty Reinsurance, who first recruited her at Antares and has continued to follow her career. She will work with Hughes as Rokstone develops its global treaty portfolio across Marine, Energy, Terrorism, Property, Aviation and Space.

The appointment comes as Rokstone continues to expand its Specialty Reinsurance operation following its first year in business. The company reported USD $25 million in gross written premium (GWP) during the division’s first ten months and has set a target of $40m in GWP for 2027. Rokstone said Isted’s appointment will strengthen the team’s underwriting capabilities as it works towards its wider business objectives.

Hughes commented: “Airlie is one of the most gifted underwriters I know and in my view is a decade ahead of her peers. I first hired her at Antares, so I have had the privilege of seeing her talent develop first-hand. Her technical ability, commercial instinct and judgement are exceptional, and she has an instinct for the business that is rare at any stage of a career.

“I am delighted to be working with her again at Rokstone. She brings valuable experience across Marine, Energy and Terrorism reinsurance, and will be a huge asset as we continue to grow the portfolio. We have made a fantastic start, but we have much bigger ambitions, and having someone of Airlie’s calibre alongside us will be instrumental as we take the business forward.”

Isted added: “Having worked with Eddie at Antares, I know first-hand the quality of underwriter he is and the kind of business he wants to build, so the opportunity to join him at Rokstone was a really exciting one. Rokstone has an outstanding reputation in the market, and its growth, entrepreneurial culture and commitment to giving talented underwriters the freedom to develop and build their portfolios make it a hugely attractive place to be.”

The post Rokstone expands Specialty Reinsurance team amid growth plans appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.dc:creator: Kassandra Jimenez-Sanchez
item.description:

Cover Re SPC Ltd. is a fully collateralised reinsurer domiciled in the Cayman Islands and licensed by the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority under […]

The post Re announces $65m capital deployment and new executive appointments appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Re, the brand under which Cover Re, Inc. operates, has announced the execution of a $65 million investment note between its wholly owned subsidiary Cover Re SPC Ltd. and the Resilience Foundation.

Cover Re SPC Ltd. is a fully collateralised reinsurer domiciled in the Cayman Islands and licensed by the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority under a Class B(iii) insurer’s licence.

Tim McDermott will lead Cover Re’s Property and Multiline team, with Ken Kurtzman and Jack Nelson also joining the company as Chief Risk Officer and Chief Investment Office, respectively.

This second capital transfer from the Resilience Foundation follows the $100 million note executed in April, lifting note capital to $165 million as Re builds out the leadership of its Cayman-based fully collateralised reinsurer

Together, the new capital and appointments strengthen the risk, investment and underwriting functions behind Cover Re’s capacity for US and international cedants.

“A second transfer of this size shows the April note wasn’t a one-off; it’s how we intend to grow,” said Karn Saroya, CEO of Re. “Every dollar that reaches Cover Re sits in trust, ranks behind our cedants, and is visible to them. That’s the standard we’ll keep holding ourselves to as capacity scales.”

As Head of Property and Multiline, McDermott will lead Cover Re’s property and multiline underwriting, including portfolios that bundle several lines of business into a single treaty.

He will be responsible for portfolio construction and capacity structuring across these lines, with a focus on deepening relationships with insurers and managing general agents (MGAs).

McDermott joins from ERGO NEXT, acquired by Munich Re’s ERGO Group in 2025, where he was Director of Insurance Product Management, overseeing P&C product management and financial performance for commercial liability, property, and inland marine portfolios.

Previously, he spent over a decade at Munich Re managing reinsurance partnerships with tech-focused and traditional insurers.

As Chief Risk Officer, Kurtzman will manage risk for Cover Re by setting reinsurance underwriting limits, overseeing capital, and reporting enterprise risks to leadership.

With over 35 years of experience in actuarial, underwriting, and risk management, Kurtzman previously served as Vice President of Reinsurance and Risk Management at NEXT Insurance, where he led reinsurance purchasing, built the enterprise risk management framework, and managed capital and reserving.

Kurtzman has also previously held positions with Platinum Underwriters, a Bermuda-based property and casualty reinsurer, and with global reinsurer Swiss Re.

As Chief Investment Office, Nelson will lead investment strategy for cash and investment-grade assets backing Cover Re’s reinsurance obligations, managing asset allocation, liquidity, duration, collateral, and regulatory compliance.

The executive previously served as Senior Vice President and Chief Investment Officer of Everest Re Group, Ltd. from 2009 to 2021.

The post Re announces $65m capital deployment and new executive appointments appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.dc:creator: Taylor Mixides
item.description:
Strategic Risk Solutions (SRS), an independent insurance company manager, has appointed Chris Terry as Managing Director and Head of Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) and Risk Strategy, with his appointment due to take effect on 19 April 2027. The move forms part of SRS’ ongoing efforts to expand its risk advisory services, with a focus on […]

The post SRS appoints Chris Terry to lead alternative risk transfer and risk strategy appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Strategic Risk Solutions (SRS), an independent insurance company manager, has appointed Chris Terry as Managing Director and Head of Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) and Risk Strategy, with his appointment due to take effect on 19 April 2027.

The move forms part of SRS’ ongoing efforts to expand its risk advisory services, with a focus on structured re/insurance, alternative risk transfer and risk consulting for organisations with complex insurance and risk-financing requirements.

Terry will join SRS from Allianz Commercial, where he held the position of Global Head of Underwriting for ART. A qualified actuary, he has built up considerable experience in the re/insurance sector, with expertise spanning technical underwriting, commercial decision-making and relationships across the international market.

In his new role, Terry will work with Derek Bridgeman, Managing Director of European Risk Consulting at SRS, and the SRS Europe leadership team to develop the firm’s risk advisory offering and support clients seeking independent guidance on risk-financing strategies. He will take over responsibility for existing structured re/insurance advisory client relationships, ensuring continuity of service following Neil Campbell’s five years leading this area of the business. Terry will also work with SRS Titanium clients requiring specialist support with the structuring of risk solutions.

Bridgeman commented: “On a personal level, I am delighted that Chris is joining SRS. We have worked together on several transactions over the years, and I know firsthand the expertise, insight, and energy he will bring.”

He further added: “Chris’s decision to join SRS reflects the differentiated advisory platform we have built and the continued demand we see from complex multinational organisations seeking independent advice on risk financing. I would also like to recognise Neil Campbell for the outstanding contribution he has made over the last five years.

“Kathryn Anderson [Director of European Consulting], the wider team, and I have learned so much from Neil and remain hugely grateful for the support, guidance, and friendship he has shared. We are very much looking forward to welcoming Chris to SRS and working alongside him as we continue to grow and strengthen our business globally.”

The post SRS appoints Chris Terry to lead alternative risk transfer and risk strategy appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.title: US insurers forecast to sustain underwriting gains in 2026 despite economic pressures: Triple-I/Milliman
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mixides
item.description:
The US property and casualty (P&C) insurance sector is expected to maintain positive underwriting results in 2026, despite continued pressures from claims costs, natural catastrophes and economic uncertainty. This is according to the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I), a US organisation specialising in insurance research and economic analysis, and Milliman, an actuarial and consulting firm, in […]

The post US insurers forecast to sustain underwriting gains in 2026 despite economic pressures: Triple-I/Milliman appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
The US property and casualty (P&C) insurance sector is expected to maintain positive underwriting results in 2026, despite continued pressures from claims costs, natural catastrophes and economic uncertainty.

This is according to the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I), a US organisation specialising in insurance research and economic analysis, and Milliman, an actuarial and consulting firm, in their latest members-only webinar, Insurance Economics and Underwriting Projections: A Forward View.

The outlook from Triple-I and Milliman indicates that the sector is likely to remain relatively stable over the coming years, although growth could slow temporarily in 2027 as monetary policy and replacement costs influence insurers’ performance.

Underlying P&C growth, a key driver of new business premium volumes, is expected to exceed gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2026 and 2028, before falling below the wider economic growth rate in 2027. Triple-I forecasts that P&C replacement costs will rise more slowly than overall inflation in 2027 before increasing at a faster rate in 2028.

Triple-I expects the US Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy during 2027, potentially slowing GDP growth and P&C underlying growth in 2027 and 2028, particularly in homeowners insurance. Geopolitical uncertainty also remains a concern. Although the inflationary effects associated with oil prices have not intensified significantly over the past three months, Triple-I warns that the outlook could change as winter energy demand increases.

“Our latest economic outlook points to greater stability for the P&C industry, but with a temporary slowdown in 2027,” commented Michel Léonard, Ph.D., CBE, chief economist and data scientist at Triple-I. “While underlying economic conditions remain supportive, monetary policy, replacement costs and geopolitical uncertainty will continue to shape the industry’s growth trajectory through 2028.”

The sector’s net combined ratio (NCR), a measure of underwriting performance, is forecast to reach 94.0 in 2026, according to Triple-I. A ratio below 100 indicates an underwriting gain, while a figure above 100 indicates an underwriting loss. Triple-I and Milliman also expect annual net written premium (NWP) growth in commercial insurance lines to exceed personal lines by approximately three percentage points between 2026 and 2028.

Homeowners insurance continues to report strong underwriting results following several years of elevated claims costs, according to Triple-I. Preliminary loss estimates associated with Hurricane Isaias are not expected to materially affect overall profitability. However, the organisation notes that the Atlantic hurricane season continues until 30 November, leaving the possibility of further storms that could significantly affect underwriting results.

Triple-I forecasts homeowners NWP growth of 6.4% in 2026, the lowest rate since 2020. The direct incurred loss ratio for the first half of 2026 was 49%, marking the strongest first-half result in more than a decade. The improvement partly reflects lower catastrophe losses compared with the same period in 2025, when the Los Angeles wildfires significantly affected homeowners insurance performance.

Despite these improvements, Triple-I highlights the sector’s continued exposure to natural catastrophes, which can cause substantial fluctuations in underwriting results between quarters and years.

Personal motor insurance premium growth is also expected to weaken in 2026. Triple-I forecasts personal auto NWP growth of -0.6%, a decline of 4.6 percentage points compared with 2025. This would be the second-lowest annual growth rate in more than 15 years, behind only 2020. The personal auto line’s NCR is forecast at 95.5 for 2026.

General liability and commercial motor insurance remain among the most challenging segments, according to Milliman, reflecting persistent claims-cost pressures. The consultancy expects the net combined ratios for both lines to remain above 100, indicating underwriting losses, although quarterly loss ratios for commercial motor insurance are showing early signs of improvement.

“General liability and commercial auto continue to present the greatest underwriting challenges, reflecting persistent loss-cost pressures,” added Jason B. Kurtz, FCAS, MAAA, principal and consulting actuary at Milliman. “We expect net combined ratios for both lines to remain above 100, although commercial auto quarterly loss ratios are showing early signs of improvement.”

Workers’ compensation continues to record comparatively strong underwriting performance. Triple-I forecasts an NCR of 92.7 for 2026, marking the 12th consecutive year of underwriting gains. NWP growth is expected to be -0.7% in 2026, with premium levels forecast to remain broadly stable in 2027 and 2028.

“After looking at loss costs, payroll, and the direct written premium change for the first half of 2026, overall 2026 net written premium is likely to be slightly lower than premium levels for 2025,” said Donna Glenn, chief actuary and product officer at NCCI. “These results and more are now available in our latest report, State of the Line—The Latest Results in 2026.”

“While underwriting results have improved, they need to be viewed in the context of several years of elevated loss costs and significant catastrophe losses,” noted Patrick Schmid, Ph.D., chief insurance officer at Triple-I. “Performance also varies considerably by line. Against that backdrop, maintaining underwriting strength is critical to ensuring insurers have the financial capacity to pay claims, absorb future catastrophe losses and support the availability of coverage.”

The post US insurers forecast to sustain underwriting gains in 2026 despite economic pressures: Triple-I/Milliman appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.dc:creator: Saumya Jain
item.description:
Reinsurance broker Howden Re has revealed it advised global insurer Generali on establishing its Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, of which Apollo acted as managing agent. It has been confirmed that Howden Re was appointed as Generali’s exclusive adviser on the transaction. The broker’s teams across Howden Re International, Howden Re Capital Solutions, and Howden Capital […]

The post Howden Re advises Generali on Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, Apollo named managing agent appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Reinsurance broker Howden Re has revealed it advised global insurer Generali on establishing its Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, of which Apollo acted as managing agent.

It has been confirmed that Howden Re was appointed as Generali’s exclusive adviser on the transaction.

The broker’s teams across Howden Re International, Howden Re Capital Solutions, and Howden Capital Markets & Advisory worked as an integrated unit to support the development of the reinsurance proposition, access to the Lloyd’s market, capital structuring, and strategic advisory services.

To recap, the new syndicate will assume a share of Generali’s outward reinsurance placements, across multiple lines of business, and has received approval in principle from the Council of Lloyd’s and is progressing towards launch.

Additionally, as previously highlighted, the platform aims to provide a strategic route into the Lloyd’s market and is part of Generali’s long-term approach to managing risk, aligning with its “Lifetime Partner 27: Driving Excellence” strategic plan.

Massimo Reina, Chief Executive Officer, Howden Re International, commented, “This transaction demonstrates the value of combining deep insurance sector expertise with a strong understanding of Lloyd’s capital.

“Working as one team across Howden, we have supported Generali in creating a tailored platform designed to broaden its strategic options and attract third-party support from across the Lloyd’s capital ecosystem. Interest in the opportunity reflects the continued appeal of the Lloyd’s market to a diverse range of capital providers.”

Vijay Mavani, Managing Director, Howden Capital Solutions, added, “This transaction demonstrates the value of the integrated Howden platform, combining deep reinsurance expertise, capital solutions capabilities and a strong understanding of Lloyd’s capital.

“Working closely with Philipp Kusche and colleagues across Howden Capital Markets & Advisory, we have operated as one team to support Generali in creating a tailored platform designed to broaden its strategic options and facilitate access to capital from across the Lloyd’s ecosystem. The level of interest in the opportunity highlights the continued attractiveness of the Lloyd’s market to a diverse range of capital providers.”

It can be said that this transaction also highlights Lloyd’s continued strength as a global marketplace, as it brings together underwriting expertise, specialist risk transfer, and capital.

The post Howden Re advises Generali on Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, Apollo named managing agent appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.title: RLI reports $58.8m underwriting income for Q3’26 as gross premiums written rise 2%
item.dc:creator: Kane Wells
item.description:
RLI Corp. has reported Q3 2026 underwriting income of $58.8 million, with gross premiums written increasing 2% to $522.2 million for the period, supported by growth in its casualty and surety businesses. The firm’s operating earnings rose to $79.3 million in Q3 2026 from $75.8 million a year earlier, while the combined ratio stood at […]

The post RLI reports $58.8m underwriting income for Q3’26 as gross premiums written rise 2% appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
RLI Corp. has reported Q3 2026 underwriting income of $58.8 million, with gross premiums written increasing 2% to $522.2 million for the period, supported by growth in its casualty and surety businesses.

The firm’s operating earnings rose to $79.3 million in Q3 2026 from $75.8 million a year earlier, while the combined ratio stood at 86.2%, compared with 85.1% in Q3 2025.

RLI’s gross premiums written increased from $510.2 million in the same period last year, with casualty continuing to account for the largest share of business.

Notably, casualty premiums rose 4.4% to $330.9 million, while surety premiums increased 1.1% to $38.9 million. Meanwhile, property premiums declined 1.5% to $152.4 million.

As mentioned, the firm’s underwriting income totalled $58.8 million in Q3 2026, down slightly from $60.5 million a year earlier.

RLI said that results in both periods benefited from favourable development in prior-year loss reserves, which contributed a net $20.1 million to underwriting income in the latest quarter, compared with $13.7 million in Q3 2025.

In Q3 2026, property remained the largest contributor to underwriting income, generating $50.5 million, broadly unchanged from the $50.4 million recorded a year earlier. Its combined ratio improved marginally to 60.1% from 60.2%.

The surety segment recorded underwriting income of $7.3 million in Q3 2026, up from $5.6 million in the prior-year quarter, while its combined ratio improved to 79.8% from 85%.

In contrast, casualty underwriting income declined to $1 million in Q£ 2026 from $4.5 million, and its combined ratio deteriorated to 99.6% from 98.2%.

Across the business, RLI’s 86.2% combined ratio in Q3 2026 compared with 85.1% in Q3 2025, reflecting the lower contribution from casualty despite stronger property and surety results.

Net investment income provided further support, rising 13% to $46.7 million in Q3 2026. However, net earnings fell 35% to $81 million, against $124.6 million a year earlier.

RLI Corp. President & CEO Craig Kliethermes commented, “Our third-quarter results reflect consistent, disciplined execution across the business. We delivered an 86 combined ratio, with strong underwriting performance in our property and surety segments.

“Gross premiums written increased 2%, led by our casualty segment. Investment income grew 13%, further contributing to earnings. As market conditions evolve across our portfolio, we remain focused on risk selection and profitable growth.

“We will continue to pursue opportunities where our underwriting expertise can deliver attractive long-term returns.”

item.title: Unrest in France underlines cat-like risks of riots and civil commotion: Morningstar DBRS
item.dc:creator: Kane Wells
item.description:
Morningstar DBRS has warned that the latest unrest in France reinforces a growing trend of riots and civil commotion increasingly exhibiting characteristics traditionally associated with catastrophe risks. “The principal concern for insurers is not necessarily the severity of an individual claim. Rather, it is the potential aggregation of thousands of correlated claims across commercial property, […]

The post Unrest in France underlines cat-like risks of riots and civil commotion: Morningstar DBRS appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Morningstar DBRS has warned that the latest unrest in France reinforces a growing trend of riots and civil commotion increasingly exhibiting characteristics traditionally associated with catastrophe risks.

“The principal concern for insurers is not necessarily the severity of an individual claim. Rather, it is the potential aggregation of thousands of correlated claims across commercial property, motor, government property and business interruption portfolios when unrest spreads rapidly across several cities,” the firm said in a new statement.

Yesterday, Morningstar DBRS reported that France’s latest riots are expected to cost insurers under €1.2 billion, assuming no further violence.

The agency said the latest unrest highlights the need to treat strikes, riots and civil commotion (SRCC) as an accumulation risk requiring dedicated pricing, limits and reinsurance.

It noted that similar accumulation effects have occurred in the United States, Chile and South Africa, where individual episodes of civil unrest have generated insured losses exceeding $2 billion.

“Repeated episodes of civil unrest are likely to maintain pressure on SRCC pricing, limits, deductibles and underwriting,” Morningstar DBRS continued.

The agency also pointed to France’s pending state-backed riot insurance mechanism as evidence of a changing perception of the risk. Once implemented, Morningstar DBRS said this mechanism should reduce uncertainty surrounding the allocation of extreme riot losses.

“Until then, however, French insurers remain reliant on the existing combination of private insurance, reinsurance and potentially contentious State recourse, reinforcing our view that civil commotion can no longer be treated as an incidental property peril, particularly in France,” the firm concluded.

Beyond the direct impact on insurers, the unrest also poses potential fiscal and sovereign risks for France, according to Mehdi Fadli, Senior Vice President, Sector Lead, Global Sovereign Ratings, at Morningstar DBRS.

Fadli went on, “While the direct fiscal costs associated with the recent protests are likely to remain manageable, the more significant risk lies in the potential for prolonged social tensions to further constrain policymaking, complicate the adoption of a 2027 budget consistent with the government’s fiscal objectives, and increase the risk that France fails to address its fiscal imbalances.

“In turn, sustained political and social pressures could keep sovereign borrowing costs elevated and further challenge fiscal consolidation efforts ahead of the 2027 presidential election.”
